body_text: As summer temperatures climb and heatwaves become increasingly difficult to escape, air conditioning can feel like an essential part of staying comfortable. Whether you are working in an air-conditioned office, sleeping in a cool bedroom, travelling in a car or staying in a hotel, a blast of cold air can provide welcome relief from the heat. However, spending long periods in air-conditioned environments may also have some less obvious effects on your body. According to doctors quoted in recent health guidance, reduced humidity, cold airflow and poorly maintained air-conditioning systems can contribute to problems affecting the skin, eyes, nose, throat and respiratory system. The good news is that many of these effects can be reduced with a few simple changes. 1. Air conditioning can make your skin dry One of the most noticeable effects of prolonged exposure to air conditioning is dry skin. Air-conditioning systems commonly reduce humidity indoors. While lower humidity can make hot temperatures feel more comfortable, it can also increase moisture loss from the skin. People who already have sensitive or dry skin may notice the effects more quickly. Common symptoms can include tightness, flaking, irritation and chapped lips. For some people, existing skin conditions such as eczema may also become more uncomfortable. A simple way to protect your skin is to apply moisturiser regularly, particularly before spending several hours in an air-conditioned environment. Products containing humectants such as glycerin or hyaluronic acid can help attract and retain moisture. 2. Your eyes may become dry and irritated Dry indoor air can affect the eyes as well as the skin. People spending long periods directly beneath an air-conditioning vent may notice burning, stinging or a gritty sensation. Contact-lens wearers can be particularly susceptible to discomfort because lenses can make existing dryness more noticeable. Blinking regularly can help keep the surface of the eyes lubricated. If dryness continues, suitable lubricating eye drops may provide relief. Contact-lens users may also find it more comfortable to reduce the amount of time they wear their lenses while spending long periods in very dry environments. If you experience persistent eye pain, significant redness or changes in vision, it is important to seek professional medical advice rather than assuming air conditioning is the cause. 3. A dry nose and throat can become uncomfortable Your nose and throat rely on moisture to function comfortably. When indoor air becomes particularly dry, these areas can become irritated. This may result in a dry or sore throat, blocked nose or hoarse voice. In some cases, dryness inside the nose can cause the delicate tissue to crack, making minor nosebleeds more likely. Dr Lucy Hooper, a London-based GP quoted in the source article, also highlighted the role of mucus in the body's natural defence system. When nasal passages become dry, clearing mucus can become more difficult. Staying hydrated throughout the day can help. It can also be useful to avoid having cold air blowing continuously across your face. 4. Poorly maintained air conditioning can affect breathing The condition of an air-conditioning system matters. A properly maintained system can help make indoor environments more comfortable, but poorly maintained units may circulate particles such as dust, pollen and mould. These irritants can be particularly troublesome for people who have allergies or respiratory conditions. For anyone with asthma or another existing lung condition, exposure to airborne irritants may potentially worsen symptoms. Home air-conditioning units should therefore be cleaned and serviced according to the manufacturer's instructions. Filters should also be replaced or cleaned when required. In offices, hotels and other shared buildings, maintenance is generally outside an individual's control. If you notice that an air-conditioned environment consistently causes coughing, wheezing or breathing difficulties, consider moving to a different area and speak to a healthcare professional if symptoms persist. 5. Cold air and dehydration may contribute to aches and headaches Have you ever left a heavily air-conditioned room with a headache or felt stiff after spending hours in a cold environment? There can be several possible explanations. Dehydration is one important factor, particularly during hot weather when your body is already losing fluid. Cold airflow may also contribute to muscle tension, especially when it is directed continuously at one part of the body. Rather than assuming the air conditioning itself is solely responsible, consider your overall environment. Are you drinking enough water? Have you been sitting in the same position for hours? Is cold air blowing directly onto your neck or shoulders? Small adjustments can make a difference. How to reduce the health effects of air conditioning You do not necessarily need to stop using air conditioning during hot weather. Instead, focus on making your environment more comfortable. Stay hydrated. Keep water nearby and drink regularly throughout the day, especially during heatwaves. Moisturise your skin. Apply a moisturiser before and after spending extended periods in dry indoor air. Protect your lips. A nourishing lip balm can help reduce dryness and cracking. Look after your eyes. If your eyes become dry, take regular breaks from screens, blink frequently and consider appropriate lubricating eye drops. Redirect the airflow. In a car, avoid positioning vents directly at your face or eyes. At home, adjust vents so cold air is not constantly hitting your body. Keep filters clean. Regular servicing and filter maintenance can help reduce the circulation of dust and other airborne particles. Consider indoor humidity. If your home becomes particularly dry, a humidifier may help restore some moisture to the air. It should be cleaned regularly to prevent microbial growth. Use air conditioning strategically. You may not need to run the system continuously. On some days, opening windows during cooler periods or using air conditioning only when temperatures rise may be enough to keep an indoor space comfortable. Should you stop using air conditioning? For most people, air conditioning remains a useful way of managing extreme heat. Keeping cool is particularly important during heatwaves, when excessive heat can pose genuine health risks. The key is balance. Very cold temperatures, dry air, direct airflow and poorly maintained equipment can make some people uncomfortable, but these issues can often be managed through hydration, skincare, ventilation, sensible temperature settings and regular maintenance. If you develop persistent breathing problems, severe headaches, significant eye symptoms or another concerning health issue, do not assume that air conditioning is the only explanation. Seek medical advice when appropriate. Final thoughts Air conditioning can be a valuable tool during hot weather, but spending hours in cooled indoor environments can have some unexpected effects on the body. Dry skin, irritated eyes, a sore throat, nasal discomfort and respiratory irritation are among the problems that may occur, particularly when humidity is low or equipment is poorly maintained. By staying hydrated, protecting your skin and eyes, maintaining your air-conditioning system and avoiding unnecessary direct airflow, you can enjoy the benefits of staying cool while reducing some of the potential downsides. Source: The Independent , August 13, 2026. Disclaimer: This article is for general informational purposes only and is not intended to replace professional medical advice, diagnosis or treatment. Individual responses to air conditioning can vary. If you have persistent, severe or concerning symptoms, contact a qualified healthcare professional.

title: Testing voice agents that remember
summary: Voice agents are moving from stateless calls to multi-call relationships. Here's how to QA cross-session memory before it burns a returning caller.
body_text: Two things happened in the last few weeks that quietly changed what "voice agent QA" has to cover. Assort Health raised a $120M Series C at a $1.2B valuation to scale what it calls Patient Journey Memory , a continuous record that carries context across every touchpoint a patient has with a practice. And Mem0 published its 2026 agent memory report, which argued that voice agents have a memory problem that is qualitatively different from text agents, because the caller cannot scroll back, cannot paste in context from a prior session, and cannot manually remind the agent of what happened last time. Put those together and the picture is clear. The voice agent your team launched twelve months ago was probably one call, one shot, one hangup. The voice agent your team is launching this quarter remembers the caller. It knows they called last Tuesday, that the referral is still open, that the prescription was flagged. Which means the QA process built around single-call transcripts is now missing an entire class of bug: the ones that only appear on call two, three, or seven. What changes when the agent remembers A stateless voice agent has one truth to defend on every call: does the transcript match the policy. A stateful voice agent has three: The lookup was correct. The right record was pulled for the right caller at the moment the call started. The personalization was appropriate. Using that record in the conversation actually helped the caller, and did not overreach. The write-back was clean. What the agent learned or promised on this call is what shows up next call, without silently corrupting the record. Each of those is a separate failure mode. In practice they compound: a bad write on Monday becomes a bad warm start on Wednesday becomes a wrong-account personalization on Friday. And unlike a stateless bug, none of it shows up in a single-call transcript review. Two of the three touch data that lives outside the call. All three depend on state that only exists because a prior call put it there. Assort's own description of the pattern is instructive: language preference, visit history, tone, open tasks and sentiment all carry through automatically , across channels and across every step of the patient journey. That is the aspiration for stateful voice, and it is also the surface area you now have to test. How call two differs from call one The failure modes single-call QA misses Once you accept that the unit of test is a sequence, not a call, a specific set of failure modes shows up: The wrong-account warm start. The agent opens the call already committed to the wrong customer's context. Caller ID matched a stale record, a household member is calling from the primary's number, the CRM associated the number to the wrong contact, or the model was fed a "trusted" caller value that came from the LLM's own transcript rather than from telephony. ElevenLabs' own guidance on this is that a phone number by itself isn't sufficient to authenticate a caller , and needs a second signal before granting access to account data. The stale-fact bug. The memory layer stores that the caller's insurance is Aetna. Six months later it is Cigna. The agent confidently corrects the caller. Mem0's 2026 report calls out staleness in high-relevance memories as an open research problem. That doesn't help you in production. What helps you in production is a test that fails when the agent presents stale state as fact. The overreach. The record says the caller is grieving, or has an eating disorder note, or churned two products ago. Referencing that is technically "correct" and functionally awful. Overreach is the failure mode that the vocal side of the call surfaces before the transcript does: it lands in tone, pace, and the caller's pause before the next word. The cross-caller leak. Two callers share a number. The primary is verified, the second is not. The agent uses the primary's context anyway. This is not a hypothetical for healthcare, home services, or family accounts. The ghost caller. A returning caller does not want to be recognized this time. They want to start over. Most agents cannot handle that at all, because the personalization is a warm-start prompt rather than a runtime decision. The forgotten commitment. Call one: agent promises a callback in 24 hours. Call two: agent has no idea. That is a memory bug, but its symptom is a broken promise, and the metric that catches it lives at the arc level, not the call level. None of these appear in an eight-minute transcript spot check. All of them appear in what the caller actually experienced. Why sample-based QA cannot cover this Sample-based QA already fails at scale for stateless voice agents, because a two-percent listen-through catches almost nothing that regressed since last week. Introduce memory and the math gets worse. Every call is now dependent on the state written by prior calls. The bugs are conditional: they only surface when a specific sequence occurs. A random sample almost never hits the sequence. The correct unit of coverage is the arc: a scripted set of related calls from the same persona, with the state that survives between them treated as a first-class test artifact. That is not something you can build out of transcripts and a spreadsheet. Old QA vs memory-aware QA Building test cases for stateful voice The mental model that works: think of the tests as multi-call scenarios attached to personas that persist. The persona has a phone number, a history, a set of preferences, and expected state carried over from the previous call in the sequence. Each call in the arc is scored, and the arc itself is scored on whether the state is coherent from one call to the next. A workable memory-aware test suite covers, at minimum: Identity resolution. Matched caller ID, unknown number, spoofed number, withheld number, duplicate contact, stale contact, mid-call number handoff. This is the entry-level testing checklist for any agent that personalizes at all. Warm start correctness. For every "known caller" scenario, an explicit assertion of which fields entered the prompt, which fields reached tools, and which fields stayed server-side. The pattern for stateful agents is read live, write on the end-of-call webhook : if the test cannot see what got read, it cannot verify what was warm-started from. Staleness scenarios. Deliberately mutate the backend record between calls two and three. Verify the agent picks up the change on call three and does not defend the old value. Overreach probes. For each sensitive field in the memory layer, a scenario where the agent should have that field available but should not proactively reference it. Score the audio, not just the transcript. Tone and pacing carry the overreach. Cross-caller isolation. Same number, different speaker. Different voice, different vocabulary, sometimes a language switch. Score whether the agent asked for a second signal before touching account data. Ghost-caller opt-out. Explicit test that a returning caller can say "start fresh" or "I'm calling about someone else" and be believed. Commitment coherence. Call one makes a promise. Call two references it. The commitment is a fact under test, not a nice-to-have. Memory poisoning. A caller asserts a false fact ("my policy number is X") and the agent writes it back. Call two starts with that false fact as if it were verified. Any pathway that writes caller-asserted facts into durable memory without an out-of-band verification step is a bug factory. The uncomfortable truth about most of this list is that none of it can be tested from a text transcript alone. The audio matters. The state between calls matters. The webhook payload matters. The metric coverage has to match. The simulation shape that actually works The reason simulation testing pulls ahead here is that a memory-aware suite is not really a QA problem, it is a call-orchestration problem. You need to place real calls from personas that persist, in the right order, with backend state mutated between them in controlled ways, and score each call on audio-native metrics that catch overreach and tone in addition to correctness. That is the shape Roark is built around. Simulations run over real telephony, either dialing your agent's inbound number or letting your agent dial a provisioned number, with personas that carry voices, languages, accents, pace, and background environments across a run. Scenarios are the unit of test; run plans and schedules stitch them into recurring, automated arcs. That is the substrate a memory-aware suite needs: not a one-shot dialer, but a scheduler that can place call two only after the end-of-call webhook from call one has closed. The scoring has to match. Roark's audio-native metrics score the sound of the call, not just the transcript: pronunciation, emotion, vocal stress, pace, pauses, interruptions. Overreach lives in exactly those signals. So does the false confidence of a stale-fact bug. There are 64+ built-in metrics and unlimited custom metrics, so the "commitment coherence" or "warm-start correctness" checks you care about become saved, monitored measurements rather than one-off audits. When a metric fails on a live call, an issue is filed automatically with the audio and the transcript attached. The other capability that pays for itself specifically with memory bugs is production call replay. When a real caller hits the wrong-account warm start on Tuesday, you don't just want to know it happened. You want to capture that call, mutate the state around it, and replay it against every subsequent version of the agent as a regression test. Stateful bugs are the ones most likely to come back after a prompt change or model rev, precisely because their surface area is invisible to prompt-level review. Illustrative memory-aware simulation suite What a memory-aware launch bar looks like For teams shipping voice agents that carry any state across calls, and increasingly that is most teams shipping voice agents at all, the launch bar has to expand. A pragmatic minimum: The identity resolution suite passes at your target rate across matched, unknown, duplicate, and spoofed cases. Every field the memory layer exposes to the model has a documented "may reference proactively" flag, and there is a test that fails when the agent violates it. Every write path from an agent call into durable state has a corresponding read test on a subsequent call. If nothing reads it, it should not be written. Staleness scenarios are part of the regression pack, not an ad hoc exercise before launches. The scored metric suite includes at least one audio-native measure of overreach or tonal mismatch, because transcript-only QA does not catch the caller's flinch. Production calls that fail any of the above are automatically captured and become replayable tests. Healthcare is the loudest example of this shift because Assort put a number on it, but the pattern travels. Any voice agent that says "welcome back" is now stateful. Any voice agent that opens with "I see you called last Tuesday about the water heater" is now stateful. The QA process either follows or it doesn't, and the ones that don't will meet the failure modes above at production volume before they meet them in test. If you're already thinking about this in the context of patient access or clinical follow-up, our healthcare writeup is the shortest path to the healthcare-specific version of the problem. If you're on Vapi, Retell, LiveKit, Pipecat, Bland, or ElevenLabs, the simulation, ingestion, and metric layer all connect through one-click integrations rather than a rebuild. The point of all of it is that the QA has to catch up to the product. Voice agents are no longer stateless. Test them like it.

title: European Law Enforcement Survey 2026: Key Finding Audio Brief
summary: Explore key findings from the European Law Enforcement Survey 2026, including cross-border crime, crime-terror convergence, SIGINT challenges and data fusion gaps.
body_text: In this episode, we explore key findings from our 2026 European Law Enforcement Survey, including cross-border crime, crime-terror convergence, SIGINT challenges and data fusion gaps. Cognyte’s survey of 200 law enforcement professionals reveals how crime is evolving, where investigations break down and what agencies need to stay ahead. As criminal tactics grow more sophisticated and investigations become increasingly data-intensive, many law enforcement agencies still lack the analytics and AI capabilities required to keep pace. Read the full survey results Watch it on YouTube Transcript European Law Enforcement Survey 2026 The Disappearing Physical Clue [Speaker 3] (0:00 – 0:17) Welcome to Cognite Audio Briefs, where we unpack what’s happening around the world and the forces shaping today’s security landscape. Each episode explores how technology can help law enforcement, intelligence, and military agencies turn complex data into clarity, insight, and decisive action. [Speaker 2] (0:26 – 0:32) Think about the last package you ordered online. It probably arrived in 48 hours, right? [Speaker 1] (0:32 – 0:33) Easily. Sometimes next day. It got scanned a dozen times, routed through these massive robotic warehouses, and just moved flawlessly through an incredibly complex global logistics network to land exactly on your welcome mat. [Speaker 1] (0:47 – 0:49) It is a modern marvel, really. [Speaker 2] (0:49 – 1:01) It is. You know, things a sharp-eyed investigator can just pick up with tweezers. [Speaker 2] (1:36 – 1:38) But that’s not how it works anymore, is it? [Speaker 1] (1:38 – 1:50) Not at all. If you look at the reality of modern European law enforcement today, the system isn’t dealing with a few hidden physical clues anymore. It is buckling under a completely different type of pressure. [Speaker 2] (1:50 – 1:51) Because everything is digital now. [Speaker 1] (1:52 – 1:58) Exactly. The battle has morphed from physical presence to sheer, overwhelming digital complexity. [Speaker 1] (2:19 – 2:21) The people actually on the ground doing the work. [Speaker 2] (2:22 – 2:44) Right. And our mission today is to explore this data to understand why the very nature of catching bad guys is currently drowning in data and why the old playbook is just burning to the ground. If you were wondering why you should care about the daily operational hurdles of a European intelligence unit, it’s because this shift directly impacts the security of your own community. [Speaker 1] (2:44 – 2:44) Absolutely. [Speaker 2] (2:45 – 2:58) It dictates the safety of your online shopping ecosystem and the literal mail arriving at your front door. OK, let’s unpack this. But knowing that physical clues are disappearing doesn’t really help us if we don’t know who is making them disappear. Who’s Really Behind Europe’s Serious Crime [Speaker 1] (2:58 – 2:59) Right. You have to know the players. [Speaker 2] (2:59 – 3:04) Yeah. We used to just look for massive cartels, but the data shows something much harder to track now. [Speaker 1] (3:04 – 3:13) It does. The survey breaks down the perpetrators of serious crimes across Europe, and the distribution is incredibly wide. I mean, we still have the heavy hitters. [Speaker 2] (3:13 – 3:14) The big guys. [Speaker 1] (3:14 – 3:29) Yeah. Forty-three percent of serious criminal activity is driven by massive, highly sophisticated transnational groups. These organizations operate with the logistics, the payrolls, and the budgets of a Fortune 500 company. [Speaker 2] (3:29 – 3:31) Wow. But that’s not even half the threat. [Speaker 1] (3:31 – 3:37) No, it’s not. Smaller groups, which the survey defines as three or more people, they account for 30 percent of the threat. [Speaker 2] (3:38 – 3:38) OK. [Speaker 1] (3:38 – 3:43) And then lone actors, so individuals operating entirely by themselves, make up 27 percent. [Speaker 2] (3:43 – 3:46) I have to pause on that split because it seems like a complete logistical nightmare. [Speaker 1] (3:46 – 3:47) It really is. [Speaker 2] (4:57 – 4:57) Business logic. [Speaker 1] (4:58 – 5:01) Yeah. It is a purely financial, rational market decision. The infrastructure is totally agnostic now. [Speaker 1] (6:27 – 6:28) Totally agnostic. [Speaker 2] (6:28 – 6:37) A smuggler who specializes in moving illicit goods across a border, I mean, they don’t care about the political ideology of the client holding the cash. On Monday, that smuggler uses a hidden compartment in a commercial truck to move a shipment of synthetic narcotics for a local drug kingpin. [Speaker 2] (7:15 – 7:16) Right. The geography of it. [Speaker 1] (7:16 – 7:20) Yeah, because the vulnerability of a border is almost entirely dictated by its geography. [Speaker 2] (7:20 – 7:24) That makes total sense. The survey breaks down the continent’s top cross-border threats, right? [Speaker 1] (7:24 – 7:34) It does. The top three overall are drug trafficking at 51 percent, weapons trafficking at 46 percent, and migrant smuggling at 42 percent. [Speaker 2] (7:35 – 7:40) But there isn’t just a blanket threat across the continent. The data shows a pretty massive regional divide. [Speaker 1] (7:40 – 7:47) A huge divide. If we connect this to the bigger picture, the mechanism of that divide becomes really clear. [Speaker 2] (7:47 – 7:48) OK, lay it out for us. [Speaker 1] (7:48 – 7:57) Well, in Western Europe, the primary concern is overwhelmingly drugs. Fifty-eight percent of respondents cite it as their top threat. [Speaker 2] (7:58 – 8:01) Because Western Europe represents massive affluent populations. [Speaker 1] (8:01 – 8:09) Exactly. High disposable incomes. It is the ultimate destination market for narcotics. But when you look at Eastern Europe, the pattern completely flips. [Speaker 2] (8:09 – 8:10) What’s the top set there? [Speaker 2] (15:29 – 15:37) That is a terrifying technological arms race to picture. Thank you so much for joining us on this deep dive. Keep asking those tough questions.

title: Your Startup MGA Doesn’t Have a Technology Problem
summary: Increase submissions, improve underwriting results and automate your back office with PolicyFly
body_text: We get calls from two very different groups. The first is an established MGA processing thousands of submissions, policies, and endorsements manually. Its team is drowning and growth has become an operational problem. The second is a startup MGA with no premium, great ideas and a fresh VC check in the bank. The first has a technology problem. The second has a distribution problem. Startups need to prove distribution first before buying or building technology. The Premature Optimization Trap “Do things that don’t scale.” — Paul Graham Insurance software can be an incredible force multiplier. It’s designed to solve complex, high-volume operational bottlenecks, massive endorsement volumes, complex exposure management, automated mid-term adjustments, and real-time auditability across thousands of policies. Do you know who has those problems? An MGA running a $20M book. Do you know who doesn't have those problems? A startup with zero active policies. Instead of optimizing for the “ideal future state”, just focus on distribution. The objective isn’t to build your permanent infrastructure on day one. It’s to learn what that infrastructure eventually needs to do. Your application will change. Your appetite will change. Your carrier may change. Brokers will send risks you never considered… Until you have real business, you are not automating a process—you are hard-coding a prediction. How Specialty Insurance Actually Runs So much of specialty insurance still runs manually — over email, with Excel raters and manual issuance teams behind the scenes. We have seen books reach both $5M and $30M+ before the manual operation begins to show cracks. That does not mean you should operate manually forever. It means you can get into the market, learn from actual business, and prove the model before committing to actual infrastructure. “If you’re not embarrassed by the first version of your product, you’ve launched too late.” — Reid Hoffman “But, Our Carrier Requires a System” We hear this a lot. Usually, what the carrier ACTUALLY requires is a reliable process and clean data. Can you show what is on risk? How it was priced? Whether it followed the underwriting guidelines? Can you produce an accurate bordereau on schedule? Those are the questions that matter. "But, we aren’t just an MGA. We are tech-enabled. It's our differentiator!” Great. But your agents probably do not care. They care about appetite, price, responsiveness, and whether you will actually quote the submission. Technology can improve those things. But a fully configured underwriting workbench or PAS without submissions or policies isn’t differentiation. It's just overhead. Distribution is King 👑 Go out of your way to become the easiest market for brokers to send business to. Take a competitor’s application. Take the expiring policy and analyze it. Call the broker and complete the submission yourself. Do whatever it takes to remove friction and generate real flow. Behind the scenes, your team can run manually. The customer experience should be fast and high-touch. The back office does not need to be beautifully automated. The Exception: You Know the Flow™ If you already have distribution on lock, then please IGNORE everything above… Maybe you are launching with an existing book. Maybe a major wholesaler has committed real submission flow. Maybe you’re an insurance veteran… You know your insurance factory will have orders. Call us. But letters of intent, encouraging conversations, and premium projections are not locked distribution—actual submissions (and their binds) are. Earn the Right to Scale Eventually, the manual operation will break. Submissions will overwhelm the team. Quotes will be delayed. Endorsements will create a backlog. Carrier reporting will require days of reconciliation. Now you have earned the right to solve the technology problem. Should you build or buy? That depends entirely on the product you’re trying to scale. More importantly, you can now answer the question using real workflows, real policies, and real operational pain. Wrestling with that decision? We should definitely chat… but only if you’ve figured out distribution!

title: Target Strengthens AI and UX Capabilities to Power Its Next Chapter of Growth
summary: We’re strengthening our AI and UX capabilities to advance our strategic priorities. Get to know our new chief AI officer and senior vice president of UX.
body_text: Technology is most powerful at Target when it brings together our team's expertise, creativity and care with the speed and intelligence of trusted data, AI and modern platforms. In our next chapter of growth , we’re strengthening our AI and user experience (UX) capabilities to advance our strategic priorities: leading with merchandising authority, elevating the guest experience, accelerating technology and strengthening our team and communities. On Aug. 24, Chandhu Nair will join Target as senior vice president and our first chief AI officer, bringing greater focus and coordination to AI across the enterprise. At the same time, Purvi Shah will move into the role of senior vice president of UX, reinforcing our belief that human-centered design is essential to creating experiences that feel distinctly Target. Chandhu Nair will join Target as senior vice president and our first chief AI officer. Purvi Shah will move into the role of senior vice president of UX. Together, these capabilities will help Target move from insight to action faster, while keeping people at the center of what we build. We sat down with Chandhu and Purvi to hear how they’re thinking about the opportunity ahead. Q: We’re accelerating technology to delight our guests and enable our team. What excites you most about helping bring that ambition to life? A: Chandhu: What excites me most is the opportunity to make AI real for the people who experience Target every day. The most meaningful AI stories won’t be about what happens in a lab. They’ll be about what happens on the front line — how we make shopping easier for a guest, give a team member a better tool, make a business decision with more confidence or bring a new idea to market faster. Target has distinctive strengths in its stores, merchandising and team. The opportunity is to use AI to build on those strengths and support Target’s priorities, not create a separate AI strategy. We should begin with the outcomes we want and focus the technology where it can make the biggest difference. Purvi: This moment gives UX the opportunity to engage more deeply than ever as a key part of the teams building the technology. Our role is to shape not only what people see, but the systems and decisions behind it to ensure each experience is as easy, inspiring and valuable as it can be. That’s another way Target can continue to lead through design, bringing the same thoughtfulness we’re known for in our assortment to the technology and experiences that shape how people interact with Target. Experience is everywhere at Target. It’s how a guest discovers a product, how a field team member completes a task and how a business partner works with our team. These moments are connected and powered with intelligence. When we make these experiences even better, we create more opportunity for Target to grow. Q: Why is it important to advance AI and UX together, rather than as separate disciplines? A: Purvi: UX helps us stay focused on three fundamental questions: What is the right problem to solve? Who are we solving it for? And are we solving it in the right way, given the context in which someone will use it? That context is especially important with AI as we design for both humans and agents. Intelligence may make a system more capable, but human-centered design helps make that capability understandable, useful and trustworthy. It helps us point the technology toward the opportunities that matter most and shape how a system should behave, not just how it should look. That requires what I call radical collaboration. We need product, technology, data and business teams sitting side by side with UX and the people we serve, learning and co-creating together from the beginning. Chandhu: Exactly. AI expands what technology can understand and do, while UX helps turn those capabilities into something useful. The ways we interact with technology are also becoming more integrated. Sometimes the right experience will be conversational. Other times it might involve voice, images or a more traditional interface. And increasingly, intelligent agents may interact with systems or with other agents. Powerful intelligence without a thoughtful experience can create confusion or fragmentation. An experience that looks good without the right intelligence underneath it can fall short of what people need. Advancing the capabilities together helps us create experiences that are intelligent, intuitive and useful. Q: Chandhu, what will a more focused and coordinated approach to AI make possible for Target? A: Chandhu: A more coordinated approach will help us focus on the outcomes that matter most for Target, our guests and our team. My first responsibility will be to listen and learn: spending time with our teams and seeing the business through the eyes of the guests, team members and partners. From there, we can focus on the places where AI can make a real difference. That could mean helping us understand changing guest needs sooner, improving how we manage inventory, simplifying work for our team or enabling faster, better-informed decisions. The measure of success won’t be how much AI we deploy. It will be the difference it makes for Target’s growth, the guest experience and our team’s ability to do their best work. Q: Purvi, as technology expands what’s possible, how will UX evolve to create differentiated experiences for Target's guests, team and partners? A: Purvi: The future of UX isn’t just about what people see. It’s also about shaping the systems behind the experience — how intelligence, services and operations work together in a seamless, end-to-end manner. A guest might start with inspiration on social media, move into a visual interface on our app and finish in a store or with help from a team member. UX helps make that journey feel trusted, connected, easy and delightful. And we’re holding the bar high for every audience. We want our guest experiences to reflect Target’s distinct thoughtfulness of great design — and we want that same level of thoughtfulness for our team members and partners. No matter who is interacting with Target, the experience should feel true to our brand. Q: And finally, what’s always in your Target cart? A: Chandhu: With two young kids, it’s usually Cat & Jack clothing and a gift for the next birthday party. Purvi: My kids and I are obsessed with Target’s Favorite Day flavored whipped cream. We try a new one each season, and can’t wait for peppermint and hot cocoa flavors to be back for the holidays.

title: Sal, Cape Verde: Complete travel guide
summary: Planning a trip to Sal, Cape Verde? Here is a complete guide to beaches, Santa Maria, flights, and money tips. Plan your trip and spend smarter with Grey.
body_text: Golden beaches, year-round sunshine and crystal-clear Atlantic waters have made Sal the gateway to Cape Verde for travellers from around the world. Whether you are looking for a relaxing beach escape, thrilling water sports or a laid-back island atmosphere, Sal offers the perfect introduction to this volcanic archipelago. Most visitors arrive through Amílcar Cabral International Airport before heading to Santa Maria, the island's lively resort town on the southern coast. Here, colourful streets, beachfront restaurants, local markets and a long stretch of white sand create an easy-going destination that suits couples, families, solo travellers and digital nomads alike. Beyond the beaches, Sal offers plenty to discover, from floating in the salt crater at Pedra de Lume to watching lemon sharks along Shark Bay and enjoying unforgettable sunsets over the Atlantic. This guide covers everything you need to know before visiting, including the best places to see, costs, transport, safety tips and practical travel advice. Everything you need to know about Sal Island, Cape Verde Sal Island is one of the most popular destinations in Cape Verde, located in the central Atlantic Ocean around 350 miles (560 kilometres) off the coast of West Africa. Covering just 216 square kilometres, it is relatively small and mostly flat, with a warm, dry climate and more than 350 days of sunshine each year. The island attracts visitors for its long stretches of golden sand, turquoise waters and relaxed atmosphere. It is also recognised as one of the world's leading destinations for kitesurfing and windsurfing thanks to its reliable trade winds. Popular attractions include the colourful town of Santa Maria and the famous Pedra de Lume salt crater, where visitors can float effortlessly in mineral-rich water. The best time to visit Sal is between November and June, when rainfall is low and temperatures typically range from 24°C to 30°C. These months offer pleasant weather for beach holidays, water sports and exploring the island comfortably. How to get to Sal Island, Cape Verde Travelling to Sal Island is straightforward, with most international visitors arriving through Amílcar Cabral International Airport (SID), the island's main gateway. The airport is located near Espargos, around 20 minutes from Santa Maria, where many of Sal's hotels, resorts and beaches are found. Direct flights operate from several European cities, making the island one of the easiest destinations in Cape Verde to reach. Airlines such as TUI and easyJet offer seasonal and year-round flights from cities including London Gatwick, Manchester, Lisbon, Paris and Frankfurt. Travellers from other parts of the world can usually connect through Portugal or another European hub before flying to Sal. After landing, reaching your accommodation is simple. You can book a private airport transfer in advance, take a shared minibus if available or use one of the licensed taxis waiting outside the arrivals terminal. Most journeys to Santa Maria take about 20 minutes, depending on traffic. Also read: 15 best things to do in Cape Verde What to see and do in Santa Maria Santa Maria is the beating heart of Sal Island and the place where most visitors choose to stay. Located on the southern coast, this lively beach town combines beautiful white-sand beaches with colourful streets, fresh seafood, local culture and a relaxed island atmosphere. Whether you are visiting for a few days or a week, Santa Maria offers everything you need within easy walking distance. At the centre of town is the S anta Maria Pier, where local fishermen return each day with freshly caught tuna, lobster and other seafood. Around the pier, you'll find cafés, restaurants, souvenir shops and beach bars overlooking the Atlantic. As the sun sets, the town transforms into one of Cape Verde's liveliest nightlife destinations, with traditional Morna music, Kizomba dancing and live bands filling bars such as Ocean Café and Buddy's Bar until late into the night. Popular places to stay: Hilton Cabo Verde Sal Resort: Luxury beachfront resort with pools, spa facilities and direct beach access. Meliá Tortuga Beach: All-inclusive resort popular with families, couples and longer holiday stays. Boutique hotels: Smaller guesthouses and boutique hotels close to the town centre offer easy access to restaurants, beaches and nightlife. Typical costs: Local taxi within Santa Maria: €2–€4 (about 200–400 CVE) Airport taxi to Santa Maria: €15–€20 (about 1,500–2,200 CVE) Casual meal at a local restaurant: €7–€12 per person Also read: How to avoid airport exchange rip-offs Best things to do in Sal, Cape Verde Discover the top attractions in Sal, from golden beaches and natural wonders to watersports and unforgettable island experiences. Santa Maria beach Sal’s most famous beach stretches along the coast of Santa Maria, offering soft white sand, clear Atlantic waters and a relaxed atmosphere. It is perfect for swimming, sunbathing, beach walks and watching spectacular sunsets. Pedra de Lume salt crater Located inside an extinct volcano, Pedra de Lume is one of Sal’s most unique attractions. Visitors can float effortlessly in the salt-rich waters, explore the historic salt pans and enjoy panoramic views of the surrounding landscape. Shark Bay Shark Bay offers a chance to see lemon sharks swimming close to the shore in their natural environment. Visitors can walk into the shallow waters and observe these gentle creatures with the help of local guides. Buracona Blue Eye The Buracona lagoon is famous for its natural “Blue Eye” effect, where sunlight creates a glowing blue colour inside a volcanic cave. It is one of Sal’s most photographed natural landmarks. Watersports With strong Atlantic winds and warm waters, Sal is a favourite destination for kitesurfing, windsurfing, diving and snorkelling. The island’s conditions attract both beginners and experienced water sports enthusiasts. Also read: How to plan a multi-country trip without losing money to FX fees Where are the best areas to stay in Sal, Cape Verde? Choosing where to stay in Sal depends on the type of experience you want. Most travellers base themselves around Santa Maria, the island’s main tourist hub, while quieter areas like Pontinha offer a more peaceful escape. Santa Maria: Best for first-time visitors Santa Maria is the most popular place to stay in Sal, offering easy access to beaches, restaurants, bars, shops and local experiences. It is ideal for travellers who want everything within reach, from morning beach walks to evening entertainment and seafood restaurants. Pontinha: Best for a quieter luxury stay Located close to Santa Maria, Pontinha offers a more relaxed atmosphere with upscale resorts and beachfront accommodation. It suits couples and travellers looking for privacy while still staying near the island’s main attractions. Espargos: Best for local experiences Espargos is Sal’s main town and offers a glimpse into everyday island life. It is a practical choice for budget travellers, those on longer stays, or visitors who want to experience Cape Verde beyond the resort areas. Accommodation costs in Sal Budget stays (€40–€80 per night): Comfortable hotels and guesthouses offering simple rooms, often without luxury facilities or all-inclusive options. Premium resorts (€180–€350+ per night): Luxury properties such as Hilton Cabo Verde and Meliá Dunas Resort offer pools, beachfront access and resort experiences, although some are further from local communities. Choosing where to stay depends on whether you prefer convenience, local culture or a full resort experience. Managing payments while in Sal, Cape Verde Landing in Sal means stepping into a relaxed island rhythm, but knowing how to pay for things makes exploring much easier. The local currency is the Cape Verdean Escudo (CVE), which you will use for everyday purchases such as local meals, taxis, markets and small shops. Some tourist areas also accept euros, especially hotels and restaurants. As you move around the island, you will find ATMs in popular areas like Santa Maria, while larger hotels, restaurants and shops commonly accept debit and credit cards. However, smaller businesses and local vendors may still prefer cash, so keeping some escudos with you is always useful. For travellers who want a simple way to manage spending, the Grey virtual Card can help you pay for shopping, meals and other expenses wherever Visa is accepted, giving you more flexibility while enjoying Sal. Frequently asked questions How do I get to Sal? Most visitors reach Sal by flying into Amílcar Cabral International Airport (SID), the island’s main airport. Direct flights operate from several European cities, including destinations in the UK, Portugal and Germany, making Sal one of the easiest Cape Verde islands to access for international travellers. Is Sal worth visiting? Yes, Sal is worth visiting for travellers seeking beautiful beaches, warm weather and a relaxed island escape. The island is especially popular with sun-seekers, watersports enthusiasts and visitors who want to experience attractions such as Pedra de Lume salt flats and the famous Blue Eye lagoon. What is the best time to visit Sal? The best time to visit Sal is between November and June, when the island experiences warm temperatures, minimal rainfall and comfortable trade winds. These months offer excellent conditions for swimming, sightseeing, beach activities and watersports, making it the ideal period for exploring the island. Do I need a visa for Sal? Visa requirements depend on your nationality. Many European and UK passport holders do not need a visa for short stays but must complete Cape Verde’s online EASE pre-registration before arrival. Always check the latest entry requirements before travelling, as rules can change. What currency does Sal use? Sal uses the Cape Verdean Escudo (CVE) as its official currency. Euros are also commonly accepted in tourist areas, with a fixed exchange rate of approximately €1 to 110 CVE. However, using local currency is often more convenient when paying for smaller purchases and everyday expenses. Can I pay by card in Sal? Cards are accepted at many hotels, resorts and larger restaurants in Sal, especially around Santa Maria. However, smaller shops, local restaurants and taxis often require cash payments. Carrying some Cape Verdean Escudos or euros is recommended when exploring outside the main tourist areas.

body_text: Write Streams Filters in Go. Or Don't Write Them at All Quicknode August 10, 2026 — 3 min read Quicknode Streams filters can now be written in Go, and Quicknode's AI Filter Agent turns a plain-language prompt into an optimized filter. Both are live in the filter editor today. Faster filters, especially on fast chains Go filters run in-process, 30% faster, especially on high-throughput chains like Solana and Robinhood. The gain comes from the runtime. Running a filter inside an isolated VM adds parsing and execution overhead to every invocation. Go filters skip the VM, so that overhead is gone, and at high block rates the saving compounds. The heavier the filter, the bigger the difference. The gap is widest on compute-intensive logic and large block payloads. Filter your stream without writing code Streams filters are getting easier to configure and deploy, based on user feedback. Quicknode's AI Filter Agent writes the filter for you. Open the filter editor and describe what you want in plain language: "filter all transactions and token transfers that involve addresses in my 'wallets' list" The agent returns an optimized, annotated filter using the correct fields for your selected network and dataset. It has context on the filter API, per-chain payload schemas, Key-Value Store capabilities and best practices, and a library of real-world filter templates. Read every line. Adjust anything you want. Migrating from JavaScript If you're filtering with JavaScript and want to migrate to Go for faster filtering, use the "Migrate to a Go filter" option. AI converts your current logic to Go automatically. Review the generated code, confirm the logic and return values match your JavaScript filter, then publish. Getting started 1. Open the Streams filter editor and select Go as the filter language. 2. Describe the filter you want, or migrate an existing one. 3. Review the output and publish. The docs at quicknode.com/docs/streams/filters now carry tabbed Go and JavaScript examples. Streams watches 7,000+ registered addresses across Ethereum, BNB Smart Chain, Solana, and Tron, and fires a webhook roughly two seconds after a payment confirms onchain. One pipeline, four chains, no separate tooling per chain. Read the pay3 case study Defimon monitors EVM chains for exploits and alerts protocol teams the moment one lands. The AI Filter Agent writes that first draft for you now, and Go runs it 30% faster. body_text: View All News Castellum Announces Second Quarter and First Half 2026 Financial Results August 6, 2026 First Half 2026 Revenue Increased 10% to $28.2 Million; Expects Full Year 2026 to Be a Record Year in Terms of Revenue Debt-Free Balance Sheet with $16.9 Million in Cash and a Total Backlog of $271.7 Million Conference Call Scheduled for Friday, August 7 at 10am ET VIENNA, Va., Aug. 06, 2026 (GLOBE NEWSWIRE) -- Castellum, Inc. (NYSE-American: CTM) (“Castellum,” “CTM,” “we,” or the “Company”), a cybersecurity, electronic warfare, and software services company focused on the federal government, today announced its financial results for the three- and six-month periods (“Q2” and “first half”) ended June 30, 2026. Q2 2026 Financial Highlights Revenues of $13.9 million, stable compared to $14.0 million in Q2 2025. Gross profit of $4.7 million, or 34% of revenues, as compared to $5.1 million, or 36% of revenues, in Q2 2025. Adjusted EBITDA* was $0.03 million, as compared to $0.50 million in Q2 2025. Net loss was $(1.1) million (or $(0.01) per basic and diluted share), as compared to a net loss of $(0.3) million (or $0.00 per basic and diluted share) in Q2 2025. Cash and cash equivalents as of June 30, 2026 was $16.9 million, as compared to $15.8 million at March 31, 2026 and $14.9 million at December 31, 2025. No long-term debt as of June 30, 2026. First Half 2026 Financial Highlights Revenues of $28.2 million, up 10% as compared to $25.7 million in the first half of 2025. Gross profit of $9.8 million, up 2% as compared to $9.6 million in the first half of 2025. Adjusted EBITDA* was $0.4 million, as compared to $0.6 million in the first half of 2025. Net loss was $(1.4) million (or $(0.02) per basic and diluted share), improved from a net loss of $(1.5) million (or $(0.02) per basic and diluted share) in the first half of 2025. * Q2 2026 Adjusted EBITDA excludes certain non-cash expenses, including stock-based compensation of $0.8 million and depreciation and amortization of $0.3 million , as compared to stock-based compensation of $0.5 million and depreciation and amortization of $0.4 million in Q2 2025. First half 2026 Adjusted EBITDA excludes stock-based compensation of $1.6 million and depreciation and amortization of $0.6 million , as compared to stock-based compensation of $1.7 million and depreciation and amortization of $0.8 million in the first half of 2025. See the reconciliation to non-GAAP Adjusted EBITDA chart below. Q2 2026 Operational Highlights Total backlog was $271.7 million as of June 30, 2026, as compared to $273.3 million at March 31, 2026 and $265.0 million at December 31, 2025. Qualified pipeline totaled $953.5 million as of June 30, 2026, as compared to $938.0 million at March 31, 2026. Achieved Cybersecurity Maturity Model Certification ("CMMC") Level 2 validating Castellum's advanced cybersecurity posture and eligibility to support DoW programs. Secured a directed $4.0 million U.S. Navy ADMACS modernization subcontract expanding Castellum’s portfolio of high‑value, mission‑critical U. S. Navy software modernization work. Won a position on the U.S. Navy’s $250.0 million LIIS CMDS Logistics IT MAC, providing a multi‑year pipeline of task order opportunities to modernize naval maintenance and logistics IT systems. Glen Ives, President and Chief Executive Officer of Castellum, commented, “Revenue for the first six months of 2026 grew 10% year over year to $28.2 million and gross profit increased to $9.8 million, driven by the continued ramp up of the major long-term prime contracts we won in 2025, including the NAVAIR PMA-290 Special Missions program and the NAWCAD Lakehurst MO&I award. This first half growth trajectory, combined with our total backlog of approximately $272 million and a qualified pipeline that continues to expand, gives us confidence that Castellum is on track to deliver record revenue for the full year 2026. Second quarter revenue was stable as compared to the prior year, reflecting gains from the ramp up of SSI's NAWCAD Lakehurst contract, partially offset by the expected wind down of certain contracts that contributed additional revenue in the second quarter of 2025. This revenue recognition timing factor is common in our industry. Additionally, we ended the quarter with a total backlog of approximately $272 million, which provides multi-year revenue visibility. We currently expect to recognize approximately 16% of this backlog over the next 12 months and approximately 48% over the next 24 months, with the remainder recognized thereafter.” David Bell, Chief Financial Officer of Castellum, noted, “Our first half results reflect the strength of the underlying business, with revenue up 10% and gross profit up 2% year-over-year. Our second quarter gross margin of 34.0% reflects a higher mix of subcontractor work, which typically carries a lower margin than direct labor, as well as the cost to complete the remaining work on the two firm-fixed-price contracts referenced above. As expected, EBITDA declined from prior periods, reflecting the planned 2026 investments in business development, investor relations, and acquisition activities. The economics of this work are inherently front-loaded. Whether we are pursuing a contract award, developing a product, or acquiring a business, certain costs are recognized well in advance of the revenue it is intended to generate. We are investing in Castellum’s future, which means lower near-term EBITDA in exchange for a stronger multi-year growth profile. Importantly, we funded the business entirely from operating cash flow during the first half, ending the period with a debt-free balance sheet and $16.9 million in cash, an increase of $2.0 million since year end, giving us the flexibility to invest in growth while maintaining a solid financial profile. With our first-half momentum and the investments we have made, we remain on pace for record full-year revenue.” Discussing the go-forward strategy, Mr. Ives concluded, “Our priorities in Phase 3 of Castellum's evolution remain unchanged, and the first half of 2026 was about putting the resources behind them. Based on the momentum we are seeing in our backlog, pipeline, and contract awards, we expect to deliver record revenue for the full year, and our focus for the second half is translating that growth into durable, higher-margin performance. Converting our backlog and pipeline into organic revenue growth. We expanded our business development capacity this year specifically to increase the volume and quality of opportunities we pursue, and that investment is already contributing to the growth we are seeing in the first half, which we expect to continue through the remainder of the year. Selectively pursuing M&A opportunities that meet our criteria. Our standards have not changed. We are looking for businesses that bring differentiated capability, contract vehicles or customer access we do not already have, and a valuation that is accretive to shareholders. We would rather pass on a transaction than force one. We continue to invest in mission-critical technologies and capabilities that expand both our addressable market and our client base. We are doing that work from a position of financial strength, funded internally and without leverage, which is what allows us to invest through the cycle rather than react to it. As we move through the second half of 2026, disciplined execution remains the priority. We believe that discipline, applied consistently, is what positions Castellum for sustainable long-term growth and enhanced shareholder value.” Conference Call Castellum will hold a conference call on Friday, August 7, 2026, at 10:00 am Eastern Time to discuss its second quarter 2026 financial results. The archived version of the webcast will be available on the Company’s website shortly after the call at www.investors.castellumus.com in the Investor Relations section under Events and Presentations. About Castellum, Inc. Castellum, Inc. (NYSE-American: CTM) is a technology company focused on leveraging the power of information technology to help solve our Nation’s most pressing national security challenges.
